corrections.tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 (MSVC supported but occasionally buggy per the README). Policy-based inline buffer and ownership (zoo::AnyContainer, AnyCallable, Function), so capacity is a template choice; zoo::function is AnyCallable<Any, Signature>. Size against std::function in the tt-metal raw outputs: 32 vs 32 bytes under libstdc++ and 40 vs 48 under libc++ (the evaluation's '24 to 32' compares zoo with its own earlier VTableFunction, not std::function). Does not build under -fno-rtti; needed a roughly 45-line wrapper to satisfy tt-metal's compliance checks. Throwing-move targets are placed on the heap (BuilderDecider in VTablePolicy.h at the pinned 7fb5eed), contrary to the evaluation's claim that they would terminate. The README's CppCon 2022 note says the released implementation may not be production-ready.
corrections.caveats: Enricher: results/summary.txt comes from a different run than results/out-*.txt (e.g. MoveOnly std 42.69 vs 42.3 ns), though the ratios agree within about 1%. The host was loaded (load average 4.2-5.6) and the reported clock varied from 2133 to 3397 MHz across configurations; partial hardware only (32 threads, 48 KiB L1d, 1.25 MiB L2 per core). The libc++ baseline makes 2 allocations, not 3. Source gotchas: converting assignment destroys the old target before building the new one, so a throw leaves undefined behaviour; a moved-from Function stays engaged; the repo's own bench 'folly' column is only a std::function alias.

tier_reason: C stands: the CCS 2017 paper is still unopened (arXiv blocked), so every number is snippet-only.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Seen only in WebSearch snippets of the CCS 2017 paper: FreeGuard averages 1.8% runtime overhead (arithmetic mean; 1.4% geometric mean) relative to the default Linux (glibc) allocator over 19 multithreaded applications, against OpenBSD malloc 34% (arithmetic) or 22% (geometric) and DieHarder 88% (arithmetic) or 36% (geometric); canneal and freqmine exceed 10% overhead under FreeGuard. A later patent for the group's Guarder allocator quotes DieHarder 74%, OpenBSD 31% and FreeGuard 1% from a different setup. The win is against secure allocators (DieHarder, OpenBSD); against glibc it is near parity (about 2% slower), not faster.
corrections.caveats: Enricher: the earlier claim text compared FreeGuard's arithmetic mean with the rivals' geometric means; compare like with like (above). Security bugs in the code: malloc(SIZE_MAX) size overflow (issue #1, closed 2021, no commit since 2018), an unchecked calloc multiplication, a time(NULL) seed (issue #2), aligned_alloc, valloc and pvalloc return NULL (so C++17 aligned new fails) and a wrong memalign formula. Quality bugs from source reading (not tested): thread_create lacks a return statement, nothing guards past 128 live threads, and the thread index comes from the stack address, so fibers or sigaltstack map to thread 0 and race its bump pointer. The Makefile uses clang++, not the paper's GCC 4.9.1.

Enricher: harness defects: the no-reserve loop always runs first in a fresh process and the order is never swapped, so first-use costs (page faults, allocator warm-up) land on the baseline side; neither vector is read after timing and there is no optimisation barrier, so an optimised build may shrink the timed work; timing uses high_resolution_clock rather than steady_clock.

Enricher: the root CMakeLists.txt never builds this chapter (#add_subdirectory(ch05) is commented out and the real folder is ch05-stack-and-heap), so the book's build was by hand. fill() writes the row number into each row, not a running counter. Size and index arithmetic in int overflows above about 2.1e9 elements, and malloc is unchecked. Setup is identical in both modes, so the traversal-only ratio must exceed the relayed 3.0x.
